paragraphs: This paper studies regression in which both the input and output are vectors, connected by a low-rank matrix plus noise. The central challenge is a particularly data-scarce setting: the number of observations is smaller than the combined input and output dimensions. Existing algorithms generally target settings with substantially more observations, with sample sizes scaling with both the matrix rank and those dimensions.

The proposed algorithm separates estimation into two stages. It first estimates the precision matrix of the input features, then solves a matrix denoising problem. Its computational structure is simple, requiring only two singular value decompositions. The authors establish statistical guarantees for this approach and introduce techniques for proving lower bounds on what any algorithm can achieve in the same problem.

These upper and lower bounds address both achievable performance and fundamental estimation difficulty. Preliminary experiments provide additional evidence: the algorithm often beats the existing baseline and remains competitive in the reported comparisons. That empirical conclusion is explicitly preliminary, while the theoretical contribution addresses learning in the unusually small-sample regime.
neurips-2020-adaptive-reduced-rank-regre.tldr: A two-SVD algorithm provides statistical guarantees for low-rank regression when observations are fewer than the combined input and output dimensions.

paragraphs: AttendLight tackles traffic signal control with a single reinforcement learning model that can serve different intersection layouts and traffic patterns. The motivation is that earlier approaches require training again when the intersection structure or traffic distribution changes. Sharing a model across configurations could make learned signal control more broadly usable.

The architecture uses two attention mechanisms to handle variable-sized inputs and decisions. One accommodates different numbers of roads and lanes; the other supports choosing among different numbers of signal phases. This flexibility comes with a stated condition: an intersection configuration must have a similar configuration represented in the training set. The model's universality therefore depends on the coverage of its training environments.

Experiments use synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets with varied road directions, lane counts, phases, and traffic flows. They examine both training and deployment in a single environment and training and deployment across multiple environments. AttendLight outperforms classical and other reinforcement learning approaches in every reported case across both regimes, supporting the value of its shared attention-based design.
neurips-2020-attendlight-universal-atten.tldr: AttendLight uses two attention mechanisms to share a traffic-control policy across intersections whose configurations resemble those seen during training.

paragraphs: Visual recognition datasets often contain many examples of some classes and few of others. This long-tailed distribution can create a mismatch between training and testing label frequencies. The paper identifies a specific consequence: ordinary Softmax produces biased gradient estimates under the long-tailed setup, affecting the learning signal used to train a classifier.

The authors introduce Balanced Softmax as an unbiased extension designed to accommodate this label distribution shift. They also derive a generalization bound for multiclass Softmax regression and show that their loss minimizes that bound. This connects the proposed change to an analysis of prediction performance beyond the training data, rather than relying only on experimental comparisons.

Balanced Meta-Softmax adds a complementary Meta Sampler that estimates an optimal sampling rate for each class. The combined approach adjusts both the learning objective and class sampling. In the reported experiments, it outperforms state-of-the-art long-tailed methods on visual recognition and instance segmentation. These results support addressing the distribution mismatch through both components within the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2020-balanced-meta-softmax-for-l.tldr: Balanced Meta-Softmax combines a distribution-adjusted classification loss with learned class sampling to improve long-tailed visual recognition.

paragraphs: Counterfactual prediction asks what outcome would occur under a particular decision, such as whether a borrower would default if approved for a loan. Historical decisions complicate this task because the factors influencing those decisions may also influence outcomes. Learning from observational records generally requires measuring all such shared factors.

The paper examines a setting in which those factors are available in historical data, but some cannot appropriately be used when making predictions. Their use may be infeasible, undesirable, or impermissible. The authors call this runtime confounding. The distinction between information available during learning and information available during deployment is the central problem the method addresses.

They propose a doubly-robust procedure for learning counterfactual predictors under this restriction, along with a validation procedure for assessing counterfactual prediction performance. Their theoretical analysis and experiments suggest that the method often outperforms competing approaches. The contribution specifically concerns restricted prediction-time access to recorded factors; its stated setting still requires the relevant factors to be captured in the historical data.
neurips-2020-counterfactual-predictions-.tldr: A doubly-robust method learns counterfactual predictions when relevant confounding factors are recorded historically but cannot all be used at deployment.

paragraphs: This paper asks how closely efficient clustering algorithms can approach non-private solution quality while satisfying differential privacy. It covers several basic problems, including Euclidean DensestBall, 1-Cluster, k-means, and k-median. The central comparison concerns approximation ratios: how much worse an algorithm's clustering objective can be than the best achievable value.

The authors give efficient private algorithms whose approximation ratios essentially match those obtainable by non-private algorithms, while adding only small additive errors. Both parts matter to the claim. Matching the multiplicative approximation quality does not mean privacy has no cost; an additional error term remains. Earlier efficient approaches achieved only large constant approximation factors, so the contribution sharpens the quality guarantees available under privacy.

The techniques also yield an improved algorithm for the Sample and Aggregate privacy framework. Separately, a tool developed for 1-Cluster supports a faster quantum algorithm for ClosestPair in a moderate number of dimensions. These consequences extend the contribution beyond the main clustering guarantees, showing that the underlying algorithmic ideas can serve other computational tasks.
neurips-2020-differentially-private-clus.tldr: Efficient private clustering algorithms nearly match non-private approximation ratios while retaining small additive errors.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks reward functions that explain demonstrated behavior. A fundamental ambiguity is that several rewards can produce the same observed behavior, so demonstrations alone need not identify the actual reward. BO-IRL addresses this ambiguity by searching efficiently for multiple reward functions consistent with an expert's demonstrations.

The framework combines Bayesian optimization with a new kernel for relating candidate rewards. Its mapping sends parameters of policy-invariant rewards to the same point in a latent space. It also makes nearby latent points correspond to rewards with similar likelihoods. This lets standard stationary kernels capture correlations across the reward search space while accounting for equivalences that would otherwise complicate exploration.

Experiments cover synthetic and real-world environments in both model-free and model-based settings. They show that BO-IRL finds multiple reward functions while minimizing expensive exact policy optimizations. The stated achievement is efficient discovery of plausible alternatives. It respects the underlying non-identifiability: recovering a uniquely correct reward still requires prior knowledge or supplementary information.
neurips-2020-efficient-exploration-of-re.tldr: BO-IRL uses Bayesian optimization and a reward-aware kernel to efficiently find multiple reward functions consistent with expert demonstrations.

paragraphs: Pairwise Markov Random Fields describe variables connected through pairwise relationships. Two central inference tasks are finding a most probable assignment, called a MAP estimate, and computing the partition function. Semidefinite programming relaxations offer a theoretically powerful route to these tasks, but the computational expense of conventional solvers has limited their practical use.

This paper makes that route more efficient by using a fast semidefinite solver based on coordinate descent. It also extends semidefinite relaxations beyond binary variables to variables with multiple classes. The authors develop a compact formulation for this broader setting that the same solver can handle efficiently, expanding the range of models the approach can address.

On benchmark problems drawn from earlier work, the method substantially improves both solution quality and speed over existing state-of-the-art approximate inference methods. The authors also demonstrate scaling to large domains, including fully connected pairwise conditional random fields used in vision. The findings support semidefinite relaxation as a practical approximate inference approach when paired with an efficient solver and formulation.
neurips-2020-efficient-semidefinite-prog.tldr: A fast semidefinite solver and compact multiclass relaxation improve the speed and quality of approximate inference in pairwise graphical models.

paragraphs: Fair classification often aims to equalize fairness measures across groups, including groups whose memberships overlap. A person can belong to several groups simultaneously, so satisfying the requirements involves considering them together. This paper revisits that problem through a probabilistic analysis of the population and identifies the Bayes-optimal classifier for the formulation.

That population-level perspective provides a common framework for several existing group-fair classification methods. It also supports extensions to multiclass settings with performance and fairness measures that are non-decomposable, meaning they cannot simply be treated as separate contributions from individual predictions. The analysis therefore reaches beyond objectives with a straightforward example-by-example form.

The optimal classifier motivates consistent learning procedures for fair classification with overlapping groups. On a variety of real datasets, the proposed approach achieves a better fairness-performance tradeoff than the baselines. This finding concerns how effectively the methods balance the two goals in the reported comparisons. The theoretical framework and empirical results together connect a population-level characterization to usable classification procedures.
neurips-2020-fairness-with-overlapping-g.tldr: A population-level analysis yields learning procedures that improve the measured fairness-performance tradeoff across overlapping groups.

paragraphs: Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization seeks decisions that perform well against the worst distribution within a specified neighborhood of a nominal distribution. For learning models, some such problems can be rewritten as tractable convex optimization tasks. Yet a tractable formulation can still be costly at scale, especially when solved using general-purpose software.

This paper focuses on a family of distributionally robust support vector machine problems. It introduces two incremental algorithms based on epigraphical projections, with iteration updates that can be computed efficiently. The authors also prove that the considered problems satisfy a Hölderian growth condition and determine its growth exponents explicitly. That mathematical structure enables convergence-rate guarantees for the algorithms.

Numerical results show speedups of orders of magnitude over the state of the art, with the gap growing considerably as problem size increases. These findings support specialized optimization as a way to make this family of robust learning problems more practical. The theoretical rates apply to the problems analyzed, while the reported speed advantages come from the numerical evaluations.
neurips-2020-fast-epigraphical-projectio.tldr: Two specialized incremental algorithms solve Wasserstein-robust SVM problems with convergence guarantees and large reported computational speedups.

paragraphs: A predictive model can change the behavior of the people it evaluates. When users understand a model, they may act in ways intended to improve their outcomes. Standard predictive training does not account for these induced decisions, so accurate predictions alone provide no guarantee that the resulting actions will improve what actually happens.

The paper introduces lookahead regularization to incorporate that interaction into learning. The model is trained to remain accurate while anticipating user actions and encouraging actions associated with improved outcomes. A central part of the framework is its treatment of uncertainty: confidence in an improvement is tailored to the distribution of actions that the model itself induces.

This makes the consequences of deploying a predictor part of its training objective. Experiments on real and synthetic data show the effectiveness of the approach. The stated mechanism encourages beneficial actions; it does not establish that every user's response will improve their outcome. Its contribution is a framework for connecting predictive accuracy, induced decisions, and appropriately targeted uncertainty estimates.
neurips-2020-from-predictions-to-decisio.tldr: Lookahead regularization trains accurate predictors while encouraging the user actions they induce to improve outcomes.

paragraphs: Funnel-Transformer targets the computational cost of maintaining a full-length sequence of token representations throughout a language model. That representation can contain redundancy, especially when the eventual task needs only one vector for an entire sequence. The paper asks whether progressively shortening the internal sequence can use computation more effectively.

Its architecture gradually compresses the sequence of hidden states, reducing computation as processing proceeds. The saved floating-point operations can then support a deeper or wider model, increasing capacity within the computational budget. To retain support for pretraining objectives that require predictions for individual tokens, a decoder recovers a deep representation for every token from the shorter hidden sequence.

Experiments show that Funnel-Transformer outperforms a standard Transformer across a wide range of sequence-level prediction tasks with comparable or fewer floating-point operations. These tasks include text classification, language understanding, and reading comprehension. The results support reallocating computation from sequence length toward model capacity, while the decoder preserves the ability to produce token-level representations when needed.
neurips-2020-funnel-transformer-filterin.tldr: Funnel-Transformer compresses hidden sequences and reinvests the saved computation in model capacity, improving reported sequence-level results.

paragraphs: Many tools attempt to explain why a neural network made a particular classification, but having an explanation available does not establish which presentation users prefer. This paper studies that user-facing question directly. It compares popular explanation methods across applications involving images, text, audio, and sensory data.

The authors conduct a comparative study with Amazon Mechanical Turk participants, asking them to compare explanation methods across those domains. Among the surveyed methods, participants preferred explanation by example in every domain except text sentiment classification. For that task, they preferred LIME's approach of annotating the input text. The exception shows that the preferred presentation can depend on the application.

The study also discusses qualitative aspects of using the examined methods and draws implications for researchers and engineers building user-facing explanations. Its evidence concerns participant preferences among the tested approaches. That makes it useful for choosing how to present model decisions to users, while keeping the finding grounded in the specific kinds of explanations and applications compared.
neurips-2020-how-can-i-explain-this-to-y.tldr: Participants generally preferred explanations by example, except in text sentiment classification, where they preferred LIME's text annotations.

paragraphs: Data augmentation changes inputs to help neural networks make robust predictions. Much of the work in this area focuses on training, while test-time augmentation often uses simple transformations. This paper proposes selecting transformations separately for each test input, making the augmentation decision responsive to the particular example being classified.

An auxiliary module predicts the loss associated with each candidate transformation for the given input. The method then applies transformations with lower predicted losses and averages the network's predictions over the resulting augmented inputs. The loss estimates therefore guide which transformed views contribute to the final answer, giving the system a learned way to choose suitable augmentations.

Experiments on several image classification benchmarks show improved robustness against various corruptions. The reported finding supports instance-aware selection as a useful part of prediction-time processing. The method combines two ideas in a single pipeline: estimating which transformations are promising for an input, then pooling predictions from the selected views to produce the classification result.
neurips-2020-learning-loss-for-test-time.tldr: A learned loss predictor selects test-time image transformations for each input, improving robustness to corruptions in benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning problems contain known symmetries relating states and actions. This paper builds that knowledge into policy and value networks through equivariance: when a state-action configuration undergoes a symmetry transformation, the network responds in the corresponding structured way. The resulting architectures are called MDP homomorphic networks.

Constraining networks in this way reduces the space of solutions learning must consider. The paper specifically studies group-structured symmetries, which involve invertible transformations. It also introduces a numerical method for constructing equivariant layers, easing the designer's task by avoiding the need to solve the symmetry constraints by hand. The authors construct both multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks with reflection or rotation symmetries.

On CartPole, a grid world, and Pong, these structured networks converge faster than unstructured baselines. The results support incorporating applicable prior knowledge into reinforcement learning architectures. The contribution combines a way to restrict networks according to known state-action structure with a practical construction method and empirical evidence of faster convergence in the tested environments.
neurips-2020-mdp-homomorphic-networks-gr.tldr: MDP homomorphic networks encode known state-action symmetries and converge faster than unstructured baselines in the reported reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often bootstraps from its own current value estimates when forming learning targets. Munchausen reinforcement learning adds another source of self-generated information: the current policy. Its central modification is to add a scaled logarithm of the policy's action probability to the immediate reward used in learning.

Applied to Deep Q-Network, this small change produces an Atari agent competitive with Rainbow without using distributional reinforcement learning, multi-step returns, or prioritized replay. The authors also combine the idea with an Implicit Quantile Network. That version outperforms Rainbow on Atari and achieves the state-of-the-art performance reported in the paper with few changes to the original algorithm.

The paper supplements these experiments with theoretical analysis linking the modification to implicit Kullback-Leibler regularization and a larger action gap. The latter concerns greater separation between action values. These insights help explain how a simple reward adjustment can meaningfully change learning. Together, the two implementations demonstrate the idea's usefulness across distinct value-learning architectures in the evaluated games.
neurips-2020-munchausen-reinforcement-le.tldr: Adding a scaled log-policy term to rewards improves Atari agents, with theory linking the change to implicit regularization and larger action gaps.

paragraphs: Object goal navigation requires an agent to find an instance of a requested object category in an unseen environment. The paper identifies exploration and long-term planning as difficulties for end-to-end learned navigation systems. It proposes Goal-Oriented Semantic Exploration, a modular system that organizes navigation around a semantic map built during an episode.

The system uses both that map and the target object category to guide exploration. Ablation analysis indicates that it learns regularities in the relative arrangement of objects and uses those regularities to search efficiently. The semantic information therefore contributes to deciding where to explore, connecting the requested category to the structure encountered in a scene.

In visually realistic simulations, the system outperforms a broad range of end-to-end and modular map-based baselines. It also led to the winning entry in the CVPR-2020 Habitat ObjectNav Challenge. The authors transfer the model to a mobile robot through its domain-agnostic module design and report similar real-world navigation performance, providing evidence that the modular approach can carry beyond simulation.
neurips-2020-object-goal-navigation-usin.tldr: A modular semantic mapping system uses learned object-layout regularities to improve goal-directed exploration in simulation and on a mobile robot.

paragraphs: Classification algorithms such as support vector machines often learn by minimizing a convex surrogate loss. They can show substantial robustness to errors in training data, and this paper asks when that behavior has a mathematical guarantee. The authors identify conditions under which surrogate-loss minimization provably learns the correct classifier.

Their analysis provides a unified treatment of multiple data and error models. A specific result assumes that the data are linearly classifiable with a margin of at least C divided by the square root of the dimension, for unit-length input vectors. It also requires the class-conditional distributions to be near isotropic and logconcave. These distributional and separation conditions are part of the guarantee.

Under those conditions, surrogate-loss minimization has negligible error on uncorrupted data even if an adversary mislabels a constant fraction of the examples. The result supplies sufficient conditions for strong resistance to label corruption. Its significance is that adversarial training errors can coexist with reliable classification when the data have the stated geometric and distributional structure.
neurips-2020-on-the-error-resistance-of-.tldr: Under stated margin and distributional conditions, surrogate-loss minimization tolerates a constant fraction of adversarially corrupted labels.

paragraphs: Louvain is a popular local-search algorithm for finding network communities: groups with dense internal connections and looser connections between groups. Its practical success is difficult to explain through worst-case analysis, which permits slow runtimes and provides no general output-quality guarantee. This paper studies its behavior in a structured probabilistic setting.

The authors use the two-block stochastic block model, where the planted communities provide a known reference for analyzing clustering. They develop tools for understanding Louvain and other combinatorial algorithms. One result gives an asymptotically tight bound on the probability that a node has more edges toward its own community, expressing the advantage above one-half through imbalance and the model's connection probabilities.

This local probability calculation helps quantify the information available to algorithms making decisions from connections. The authors identify its usefulness for Louvain, Kernighan-Lin, simulated annealing, and related analyses. The contribution described is a set of tools for explaining behavior under the stochastic block model, addressing the gap between pessimistic worst-case reasoning and the success of local search in practice.
neurips-2020-on-the-power-of-louvain-in-.tldr: Analysis in the two-block stochastic block model develops tight probabilistic tools for understanding Louvain and other local-search algorithms.

paragraphs: Ensemble methods combine models fitted to different samples of the training data and can produce accurate, stable predictions. Attaching a valid predictive interval to those predictions is a separate challenge. This paper introduces jackknife+-after-bootstrap, or J+aB, to construct intervals using bootstrapped samples and models that have already been fitted.

The procedure is described as free specifically in terms of additional model-fitting cost. It reuses the available ensemble rather than requiring new fits for interval construction. Its predictive coverage guarantee does not impose assumptions on the data distribution, fitted model type, or method of aggregating the ensemble. The guarantee allows the interval's failure rate to be inflated by at most a factor of two.

Experiments on real data verify the coverage and accuracy of the resulting intervals. The contribution is therefore both computational and statistical: existing bootstrap training can support predictive uncertainty estimates with a broad coverage guarantee. The factor-of-two qualification is central to interpreting that guarantee, while the cost claim concerns fitting models rather than every operation involved in constructing an interval.
neurips-2020-predictive-inference-is-fre.tldr: J+aB reuses fitted bootstrap models to produce predictive intervals with a coverage guarantee allowing at most twice the target failure rate.

paragraphs: The Learnable Tree Filter models relationships while preserving image structure, but its geometric constraint favors nearby regions. This makes it harder to capture interactions between distant parts of an image. The paper revisits that constraint so the filter can combine long-range information while retaining structural detail.

The authors reformulate the filter as a Markov Random Field and introduce a learnable unary term to relax the geometric restriction. They also replace the original non-differentiable spanning-tree procedure with a learnable spanning-tree algorithm. Together, these changes improve flexibility and robustness while retaining linear computational complexity. The revised filter becomes a more general feature transformation that can be applied across several vision tasks.

Experiments on object detection and instance segmentation show consistent improvements over the original filter. For semantic segmentation, the method reaches 82.1% mean intersection over union on Cityscapes, which the authors report as leading performance without additional embellishments. The results support the central design goal: improving distant interactions and preserving local structure within the same efficient filtering approach.
neurips-2020-rethinking-learnable-tree-f.tldr: A revised learnable tree filter captures longer-range image relationships while preserving structural details and linear complexity.

paragraphs: Low-bit neural networks use weights and activations drawn from small sets of values, making them attractive for AI accelerators. Training them is challenging because conventional quantization functions are non-differentiable. This paper treats the small number of possible weight values as an opportunity to search directly among discrete choices.

Each weight is represented during training by a probability distribution over its allowed values. A differentiable method optimizes those probabilities, and the highest-probability value is then selected for the final quantized network. For example, a four-bit weight has only sixteen possible values. The method uses this restricted choice set to reformulate weight learning as a search over alternatives.

Benchmark experiments show higher performance than state-of-the-art quantization methods on image classification and super-resolution. These findings support the proposed search formulation across both recognition and image reconstruction tasks. The key contribution is the training representation: probabilities provide an optimizable description of discrete weights, while selecting their most likely values produces the desired low-bit network.
neurips-2020-searching-for-low-bit-weigh.tldr: Representing each low-bit weight as a learned distribution over discrete values improves reported quantized-network performance.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning creates training targets from unlabeled data so a network can learn useful representations without manual annotation. This paper builds that training signal from relationships. A relation head learns to distinguish how entities relate to themselves and how they relate to other entities, training the underlying network through both kinds of reasoning.

The resulting backbone representations can support downstream tasks such as classification and image retrieval. The authors connect the method's effectiveness to maximizing a Bernoulli log-likelihood, which they interpret as a proxy for maximizing mutual information. This connection motivates an objective they describe as more efficient than commonly used contrastive losses.

Evaluation uses standard datasets, protocols, and network backbones. The authors report outperforming the best competitor in every evaluated condition, with an average accuracy improvement of 14%, and a 3% improvement over the most recent state-of-the-art model. These are findings within the reported evaluation. They support relational discrimination as a useful source of supervision for learning representations from unlabeled data.
neurips-2020-self-supervised-relational-.tldr: Learning relationships within and between entities produces useful unlabeled-data representations and improves accuracy in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Navigation can benefit from regularities in how real environments are arranged. This paper learns semantic cues for finding objects in unfamiliar environments from YouTube videos. Such videos present a difficult learning source because they lack action and goal labels, and the behavior they show may be suboptimal.

The method creates pseudo-labeled transitions containing an image, an action, a following image, and a reward. It then applies off-policy Q-learning to these transitions. The authors show that this passive data can provide meaningful semantic cues for navigation. Those cues are incorporated into a hierarchical navigation policy, connecting video-based learning to goal-directed movement.

In visually realistic simulations, the resulting policy improves efficiency on the ObjectGoal task while requiring minimal direct interaction. The reported relative improvements range from 15% to 83% over end-to-end reinforcement learning, behavior cloning, and classical methods. The findings support using imperfect, unlabeled videos as a source of useful navigation knowledge when pseudo-labeling and off-policy learning are combined with a hierarchical policy.
neurips-2020-semantic-visual-navigation-.tldr: Q-learning from pseudo-labeled YouTube video transitions supplies semantic cues that improve simulated object navigation with minimal direct interaction.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimal experimental design often scores candidate experiments by mutual information, but evaluating that score can be computationally expensive. Many methods substitute bounds without providing regret-style guarantees. This paper uses both lower and upper bounds, refining them through additional computation until the desired guarantee is reached.

The central decision is where to spend that computation. The authors adapt ideas from knapsack optimization for best-arm identification, while accounting for features specific to experimental design. Mutual-information reward observations are biased, and evaluation costs have two components: shared posterior-sampling costs and experiment-specific costs that can change as evaluation continues. These features shape which refinement is most worthwhile.

The proposed algorithm explicitly incorporates those variable costs into its refinement decisions. It achieves the same guarantee as existing methods with fewer evaluations of the costly mutual-information reward. The contribution links reliable experiment selection to computational resource allocation: bounds determine when enough evidence has been gathered, while the cost model guides how to obtain that evidence efficiently.
neurips-2020-sequential-bayesian-experim.tldr: Adaptive refinement of two-sided information bounds provides experiment-selection guarantees with fewer costly evaluations while accounting for shared and variable costs.

paragraphs: Sufficient dimension reduction seeks a lower-dimensional representation that retains the information needed to predict a response. Many existing approaches were developed for continuous responses and can perform poorly with category labels, especially in binary classification. This paper proposes principal optimal transport direction, or POTD, to address that setting.

POTD uses an optimal transport coupling between data associated with different response categories. It takes principal directions of that coupling to estimate a basis for the sufficient dimension reduction subspace. This makes relationships between category-specific data central to the reduction procedure. The analysis also reveals connections among sufficient dimension reduction, support vector machines, and optimal transport.

The authors study POTD's asymptotic properties and show that, when class labels contain no errors, its subspace estimation is confined to the sufficient dimension reduction subspace. That conclusion carries the explicit error-free-label condition. Empirical studies show that POTD outperforms most state-of-the-art linear dimension reduction methods, supporting optimal transport as a useful approach to supervised reduction for classification.
neurips-2020-sufficient-dimension-reduct.tldr: POTD estimates classification-relevant reduction directions through optimal transport between categories and outperforms most compared linear methods empirically.
